formulas.name: Traditional yield
formulas.conditions: misleading perspective; obscures impact of inspection and rework

formulas.name: First time yield
formulas.conditions: likelihood of an item passing through a process successfully the very first time, including effects of inspection, rework and scrap

formulas.name: Rolled throughput yield (generalized)
formulas.expression: RTY = the product (pi, i=1 to n) of FTYi

symbols.FTYi: first time yield of process step i

formulas.conditions: combined overall yield of an entire process stream; can never be greater than the lowest FTY in the system

formulas.name: Defects per unit (DPU)
formulas.expression: DPU = number of defects observed / number of units inspected

formulas.name: Defects per opportunity (DPO)
formulas.expression: DPO = number of defects observed on a unit / number of opportunities on a unit
formulas.conditions: allows fair comparison of defect rates between items of different complexity

formulas.name: Defective parts per million (DPPM)

symbols.DPPM: defective parts per million, synonymous with DPMO

formulas.conditions: used when the 'part' is the opportunity, e.g. continuous material or ongoing shipments

formulas.name: Rolled throughput yield from DPU
formulas.conditions: valid when overall process DPU is relatively low, e.g. less than 0.10 (10 percent)

formulas.name: DPU from rolled throughput yield
formulas.conditions: algebraic inverse of RTY = e^-DPU

formulas.name: Sigma (Z) score
formulas.conditions: use only on a characteristic that is approximately normal

formulas.name: 1.5-sigma shift (shifted Z)

symbols.Z_shifted: sigma score of the mathematically shifted short-term distribution

formulas.conditions: early Six Sigma practitioners proposed shifting the short-term distribution 1.5 standard deviations closer to the specification limit to approximate long-term defect performance

formulas.name: 1.5-sigma shift (long-term from short-term)
formulas.conditions: the shifted distribution is treated as defect-wise equivalent to the long-term distribution

formulas.name: Short-term capability index Cp
formulas.conditions: use only the short-term standard deviation; a long-term standard deviation gives incorrect results

formulas.name: Adjusted short-term capability indices Cpu and Cpl
formulas.expression: Cpu = (USL - xbar) / (3 x sigma_ST); Cpl = (xbar - LSL) / (3 x sigma_ST)
formulas.conditions: compares distance from distribution center to each specification limit against half-width of short-term variation

formulas.name: Adjusted short-term capability index Cpk
formulas.expression: Cpk = min(Cpu, Cpl) = min( (USL - xbar)/(3 x sigma), (xbar - LSL)/(3 x sigma_ST) )

symbols.min: choose the smallest of the values in parentheses
symbols.sigma: as printed (no ST subscript) in first term
symbols.sigma_ST: short-term standard deviation, as printed in second term

formulas.conditions: as printed, the first denominator is shown as '3 sigma' without the ST subscript while the second is '3 sigma_ST'; see ambiguities

formulas.name: Long-term capability index Pp
formulas.conditions: same formula as Cp but using sigma_LT in place of sigma_ST

formulas.name: Adjusted long-term capability index Ppk
formulas.expression: Ppk = min( (USL - xbar)/(3 x sigma_LT), (xbar - LSL)/(3 x sigma_LT) )
formulas.conditions: same formula as Cpk but using sigma_LT in place of sigma_ST

symbols.sigma^2_MEASURE: variance contributed by the measurement system

formulas.name: Confidence interval for a mean, large sample

symbols.Z: sigma value corresponding to desired confidence
symbols.sigma: calculated standard deviation from the sample
symbols.n: number of data points in the sample

formulas.conditions: works any time you have more than 30 measurements in your sample

formulas.name: Confidence interval for a mean, small sample

symbols.t: look-up factor depending on desired confidence level and number of data points (replaces Z)

formulas.conditions: used when sample has anywhere from two to 30 data points

formulas.name: Confidence interval for a standard deviation
formulas.expression: [ sqrt( (n-1) sigma^2 / chi^2_LOWER ), sqrt( (n-1) sigma^2 / chi^2_UPPER ) ]
formulas.conditions: confidence intervals for standard deviations are usually very wide unless sample size is large

formulas.name: Confidence interval for ratio of variances

symbols.sigma1^2: variance of numerator distribution (n1 data points)
symbols.sigma2^2: variance of denominator distribution (n2 data points)

formulas.conditions: if the interval contains the value 1, there is no evidence the two distributions have different variances

formulas.name: Confidence interval for a proportion

symbols.n: total number of attempts or trials

formulas.conditions: proportions can never be less than zero or greater than one; adjust interval to natural limits if exceeded

formulas.name: Confidence interval for the difference of two proportions
formulas.conditions: if interval does not include zero, conclude with the stated confidence that the two proportions differ

formulas.name: Correlation coefficient (r)
formulas.expression: r = (1/(n-1)) x sum_{i=1 to n} [ ((xi - xbar)/sigma_x) x ((yi - ybar)/sigma_y) ]

symbols.xbar, ybar: averages of X and Y measurements
symbols.sigma_x, sigma_y: standard deviations of X and Y measurements

formulas.conditions: r is always between -1 and 1; tells only how linear a relationship is, not causation

formulas.name: Simple linear regression model

symbols.epsilon: normal random distribution centered at zero

formulas.conditions: used for a system with a single output Y and single input X

formulas.name: Slope estimate for simple linear regression
formulas.expression: beta_1 = sum( (xi - xbar) yi ) / sum( (xi - xbar)^2 )

symbols.Yhat_i: predicted estimates for the n data points

formulas.name: Error sum of squares (SSE)
formulas.expression: SSE = sum e_i^2 = sum_{i=1 to n} (Y_i - Yhat_i)^2

formulas.name: Coefficient of determination
formulas.conditions: want this number to be 80 percent or higher

formulas.name: Estimated standard deviation of unexplained (epsilon) variation
F test for regression model validity
formulas.expression: sigmahat^2_REG / sigmahat^2_epsilon >= F(2, n-1); where sigmahat^2_REG = SSR and sigmahat^2_epsilon = SSE/(n-2)

symbols.sigmahat^2_REG: estimate of variance explained by regression model

formulas.conditions: if ratio exceeds the critical F value, conclude with the chosen confidence (e.g. 99 percent) that the derived model is valid

formulas.name: General multiple linear regression model (two inputs)
formulas.expression: Y_i = beta_0 + beta_1 X_1 + beta_11 X_1^2 + beta_2 X_2 + beta_22 X_2^2 + beta_12 X_1 X_2 + epsilon

symbols.epsilon: random unexplained variation, normal, centered at zero

formulas.conditions: extension of simple linear regression to more than one X

formulas.name: Number of runs in a 2^k factorial experiment
formulas.conditions: e.g. k=3 gives 2^3=8 runs; k=2 gives 2^2=4 runs

formulas.name: General main/interaction effect formula for a 2^k factorial experiment
formulas.expression: E_i = (1 / 2^(k-1)) x sum_{j=1 to 2^k} c_(i,j) Y_j

symbols.c_(i,j): coded setting value (+1 or -1, or product of coded values for interactions) for run j

formulas.name: Expected probability for normal-score ranking of effects

symbols.i: rank of the effect (smallest to largest, ties given average rank)

formulas.conditions: used as an intermediate step before looking up the corresponding Z value to build a normal probability plot of effects

formulas.name: General Y=f(X) equation for a three-factor 2^k experiment
formulas.expression: Y = beta_0 + beta_1 X_1 + beta_2 X_2 + beta_3 X_3 + beta_12 X_1 X_2 + beta_13 X_1 X_3 + beta_23 X_2 X_3 + beta_123 X_1 X_2 X_3

symbols.beta_0: overall offset/constant term (computed average of all 2^k experiment runs)
symbols.beta_i, beta_ij, beta_ijk: coefficients for main, two-way interaction, and three-way interaction effects

formulas.conditions: only terms found significant are retained in the simplified equation

formulas.name: Coefficient from effect (2^k experiment)
formulas.expression: beta_i = E_i / 2 (for any significant effect); beta_0 = average of all 2^k experiment run outputs
formulas.conditions: coefficient is half the effect value because the effect spans a coded distance of two (+1 to -1)

formulas.name: Continuous control chart formulas: Individuals and Moving Range (I-MR)
formulas.expression: Xbar = (X1+X2+...+Xk)/k; MR_i = |X_(i+1) - X_i|; MRbar = (MR1+MR2+...+MR_(k-1))/(k-1); UCL_X = Xbar + E2 x MRbar; LCL_X = Xbar - E2 x MRbar; UCL_MR = D4 x MRbar; LCL_MR = D3 x MRbar

symbols.E2, D3, D4: look-up constants depending on subgroup size (Table 10-2 constants)

formulas.conditions: subgroup size n = 1

formulas.name: Continuous control chart formulas: Averages and Ranges (Xbar-R)
formulas.expression: Xbar = (Xbar1+Xbar2+...+Xbar_k)/k; Rbar = (R1+R2+...+R_k)/k; UCL_Xbar = Xbarbar + A2 x Rbar; LCL_Xbar = Xbarbar - A2 x Rbar; UCL_R = D4 x Rbar; LCL_R = D3 x Rbar

symbols.A2, D3, D4: look-up constants depending on subgroup size (Table 10-2 constants)

formulas.conditions: subgroup size n = 2 to 10

formulas.name: Continuous control chart formulas: Averages and Standard Deviations (Xbar-S)
formulas.expression: Xbar = (Xbar1+Xbar2+...+Xbar_k)/k; Sbar = (S1+S2+...+S_k)/k; UCL_Xbar = Xbarbar + A3 x Sbar; LCL_Xbar = Xbarbar - A3 x Sbar; UCL_S = B4 x Sbar; LCL_S = B3 x Sbar

symbols.A3, B3, B4: look-up constants depending on subgroup size (Table 10-2 constants)

formulas.conditions: subgroup size n > 10

formulas.name: p chart (proportion defective)
formulas.expression: p_i = number defective / n_i (per subgroup); pbar = total number defective / (n1+n2+...+n_k); UCL_i = pbar + 3 sqrt( pbar(1-pbar)/n_i ); LCL_i = pbar - 3 sqrt( pbar(1-pbar)/n_i )
formulas.conditions: based on the binomial distribution; used for defectives (pass/fail) data

formulas.name: u chart (defects per unit)
formulas.expression: u_i = number defects / n_i (per subgroup); ubar = total number defects / (n1+n2+...+n_k); USL_i = ubar + 3 sqrt( ubar/n_i ); LSL_i = ubar - 3 sqrt( ubar/n_i )
formulas.conditions: based on the Poisson distribution; used for defect (count) data. Note: book labels the control limits USL_i/LSL_i in Table 10-3 rather than UCL_i/LCL_i

constant_tables.name: Table 6-1: Summary of Yield Metrics
rows: Is a misleading perspective that obscures the impact of inspection and rework.
Shows the likelihood of an item passing through a process successfully the very first time. Includes effects of inspection, rework and scrap.
RTY = product (pi), i=1 to n, of FTY_i
The combined overall yield of an entire process stream. Tells you the likelihood of an item passing through all process steps successfully the first time.

constant_tables.name: Table 6-2: Summary of Defect Rate Metrics
rows: DPU = number of defects observed / number of units inspected
DPU provides a measurement of the average number of defects on a single unit.
DPO = number of defects observed on a unit / number of opportunities on a unit
DPO measures the number of defects that occur per opportunity for success or failure. DPO allows you to fairly compare the defect rates of things with very different levels of complexity.
DPMO is the average number of defects found over a million opportunities. Best used when the process/characteristic is repeated many times.

constant_tables.name: Table 7-2: Measurement-to-Observed Variation Ratio Values and Interpretation
rows: Good measurement system. Contribution of the measurement system to the overall observed variation is small enough to enable good decisions from the measurements.
Use measurement system as it is. Look for opportunities to simplify or make the measurement system less expensive or more efficient.

Marginal measurement system. Contribution of the measurement system to the overall observed variation is beginning to cloud results. There is a significant risk of making a wrong decision from the measurements.

Use with caution only if no better measurement alternative exists. Begin to improve the measurement system by training operators, standardizing measurement procedures, and investigating new measurement equipment.
Unacceptable measurement system. Guessing is probably just as precise. Do not base important decisions off of information from a measurement system in this condition.
Measurement system needs to be corrected before any valid information can be derived from the system. Investigate causes of gross inconsistency.

conventions.topic: sigma estimate for capability (Cp/Cpk vs Pp/Ppk)
conventions.as_stated: Cp is a measure of short-term process or characteristic capability. Use only the short-term standard deviation to calculate its value. Using a long-term standard deviation in its calculation gives you incorrect results. ... The same capability indices that you calculate for short-term variation, Cp and Cpk, can also be calculated for long-term variation. To differentiate them from their short-term counterparts, these long-term capability indices are called Pp and Ppk. The only difference in their formulas is that you use sigma_LT in place of sigma_ST.

conventions.topic: short-term vs long-term sigma / Zst vs Zlt
conventions.as_stated: If you are using a short-term standard deviation, the sigma (Z) score you calculate is a short-term sigma score Zst... If, however, you have a long-term standard deviation, you can calculate the long-term sigma score Zlt... Short-term variation performance, as quantified by the short-term sigma score Zst, represents the best variation performance that you can expect out of your currently configured process. It is an idealistic measure of capability.

Early practitioners of Six Sigma proposed that mathematically shifting a characteristic's or process's short-term distribution closer to its specification limit by a distance of 1.5 times its short-term standard deviation (sigma_ST) would approximate the amount of defects occurring in the long term. ... Zlt = Zst - 1.5.

See Table 6-3 (transcribed in constant_tables) and its printed note: paired table values are long-term for DPMO and short-term for Z; add 1.5 to corresponding Z values to obtain short-term equivalents.

Generally, a CPK greater than 1.33 indicates that a process or characteristic is capable in the short-term. Values less than this tell you that the variation is either too wide compared to the specification or that the location of the variation is offset from the center of the specification. Or it may be a combination of both width and location.
Confidence interval for a standard deviation uses (n-1) sigma^2 in the numerator together with chi-square lower/upper look-up values (Table 8-2), i.e. based on n-1 degrees of freedom.

The book ties confidence directly to standard-deviation multiples: 68% corresponds to Z=1 (or t/chi2/F look-ups for one standard deviation), 95% to Z=2, and 99.7% to Z=3. Tables 8-1, 8-2, and 8-3 are built around these three levels (F table given only for 95%). No single universal alpha/confidence default is stated beyond these three illustrative levels.
The risk of incorrectly concluding that the population average is within your calculated confidence interval when, in reality, it is not, is called alpha (a) risk.

Valid estimates of the variance of the measurement system usually involve two to three inspectors and five to ten process outputs or characteristics to measure. Each inspector also measures each process output or characteristic two to three times.

Set aside 15 to 30 samples (about half pass, half fail); create a 'master' standard via a panel of experts; pick two or three inspectors; have each inspector repeat measurements after randomizing order; calculate percentage agreement of first vs second measurements per inspector (repeatability), and agreement across inspectors and with the master standard (reproducibility). Example given: a calculated 63 percent agreement between all inspectors for all samples with the 'master' standard means there is a 63 percent likelihood the measurement system will correctly measure items and a 37 percent chance of error.

sigma^2_measure/sigma^2_observed <= 0.1: good measurement system, use as is. 0.1 to 0.3: marginal, use with caution only if no better alternative exists. >= 0.3: unacceptable measurement system, must be corrected before use.

Using -1s as a code for the 'low' variable settings and +1s as a code for the 'high' settings, start with the left-most variable column, and fill in the column cells with alternating -1s and +1s. With the left-most column filled in, move on to the next column to the right and repeat the process -- but this time with alternating pairs of -1s and +1s. Fill in the next column to the right with alternating quadruplets of -1s and +1s, and so on. This table of patterned +1s and -1s is called coded design matrix.

The beta value for all... significant factors is found by dividing the corresponding effect value in half... It's because the effect value is calculated over a span of +1 to -1 for the variable. That's an effective distance of two, not one. Therefore, to get back to the right equation coefficient, you have to divide the calculated effect value by two.

Always randomize the order of your experiment runs. This reduces the risk of extraneous variables skewing the results of your analysis. ... A catchy phrase may help you remember the roles of randomizing and blocking in your experiments: Block what you can and randomize against what you can't block.

There is an upper control limit (UCL): It's typically three process standard deviations above the average. There is a lower control limit (LCL): It's typically three process standard deviations below the average. ... Plus or minus three standard deviations from the mean includes 99.7 percent of all the data in a normally distributed population.

conventions.topic: control chart run rules (special-cause zone tests)
conventions.as_stated: Any one point beyond either control limit. Two out of any three consecutive points in Zone A, and all three on the same side of the process average. Four out of any five consecutive points in Zone B or A, and all five on the same side of the process average. Fifteen points in a row in Zone C, on either side of the process average.

Stable and predictable: chart points do not form a particular pattern and lie within upper/lower control limits -> only common-cause variation. Beyond control limits: one or more points lie beyond UCL/LCL -> investigate special cause. Run: chart points on one side of centerline -> process has undergone a permanent change, may require recomputing control limits. Trend: continued rise or fall in a series of points (seven or more consecutive points in the same direction) -> gradual, cumulative special cause. Cycle: same pattern changes over equal periods of time -> cyclical, repetitive special cause. Hugging: points close to centerline or to a control limit line -> possible error in data subgrouping or selection.

conventions.topic: control limits are not specification limits
conventions.as_stated: Never confuse control chart limits with specification limits! Specification limits -- like the USL and LSL introduced in Chapter 6 -- represent the voice of the customer. Control charts, however, represent only the voice of the process... control charts only determine whether the process is stable and predictable. They do not tell you whether the process is capable of meeting customer requirements.

Rational subgroups are usually small in size, typically consisting of three to five measurements. ... After you have collected a minimum of 25 subgroups of data (with 2 to 5 measurements in each subgroup), you can calculate the statistics and control limits.

conventions.topic: continuous control chart pairing / choice by subgroup size
conventions.as_stated: Individuals and moving range (I-MR): subgroup size (n) = 1. Averages and ranges (Xbar-R): subgroup size 2-10. Averages and standard deviations (Xbar-S): subgroup size > 10. Use the Xbar-S chart when the size of your subgroups is ten measurements or greater, and the Xbar-R when they are less than ten.

conventions.topic: attribute control chart selection (p vs u)
conventions.as_stated: If you're charting defectives attribute data (pass/fail, go/no-go, acceptable/unacceptable), you use a p chart. ... If you're counting and keeping track of the number of defects on an item, you're using defect attribute data, and you use a u chart to perform statistical process control. p charts for defectives data are based on a binomial distribution. u charts for defects data are based on the Poisson distribution.

The most effective form of process control is sometimes called a Type-1 corrective action. This is a control applied to the process that eliminates the error condition from ever occurring. This is the primary intent of the Poka-Yoke method. The second most effective control is called a Type-2 corrective action. This is a control that detects when an error occurs and stops the process or shuts down the equipment so that the defect cannot move forward. This is the detection application of the Poka-Yoke method.

ambiguities.issue: Table 6-3 footnote wording is internally confusing as printed: 'Note: Paired table values are long-term for DPMO and short-term for Z (example, a long-term DPMO of 6,210 is the result of a process with a short-term sigma score of 4.0). Add 1.5 to corresponding Z values to obtain short-term equivalents (example, a short-term DPMO of 32 is the result of a process with a short-term sigma score of 4.0).' Both examples cite 'a short-term sigma score of 4.0' even though the second example's DPMO (32) corresponds to the table row Z=5.5 (=4.0+1.5), which is inconsistent-looking; transcribed exactly as printed.
